Photograph: Aaron Bunch/AAP View image in fullscreen A staff member at a residential care home west of Brisbane is accused of assaulting the girl on 20 August. Photograph: Aaron Bunch/AAP Queensland Teenage girl allegedly raped in ‘heinous’ attack at Queensland residential care home State’s child safety minister Amanda Camm confirms police are investigating alleged attack west of Brisbane Australian Associated Press Wed 26 Aug 2026 01.03 EDT Last modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 01.18 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Queensland teenager has allegedly been raped in a state-funded residential care home in what has been described as a “heinous” act. A staff member is accused of assaulting the girl, who is understood to be intellectually impaired, at the home west of Brisbane. Queensland’s child safety minister, Amanda Camm, confirmed the alleged attack was being investigated and said she had zero tolerance for abuse, “particularly when it comes to vulnerable children in care”. “Queenslanders would rightly expect that anyone convicted of such [an allegedly] heinous offence deserves to face the full force of the law,” she told reporters on Wednesday. Detectives have been investigating the alleged 20 August assault at the home. The out-of-home residential care provider, which serves vulnerable children and young people, has been contacted for comment. The acting deputy police commissioner Rhys Wildman confirmed an investigation was under way, but declined to provide further detail, citing the alleged victim’s vulnerability. Child safety system ‘broken’ Pressure about the child safety system has been mounting on Camm, after the Liberal National party government claimed it was “broken” before it came into power. Camm said a commission of inquiry in June found about 67% of reported sexual exploitation in state care involved children in residential care. “Sixty-seven per cent of children in residential care that have reported sexual abuse allegations is unacceptable,” she said, adding the government did “not have a moment to waste” in reforming the system. Camm said contracts had been cancelled where residential care providers failed to meet safety and quality standards, and that such providers “have no place” in the system. The government also responded to 52 recommendations made in the child safety inquiry’s final report , accepting 32 of them while committing $200m to implement them within 30 months. The 11-month inquiry’s report exposed years of systemic failure, revealing no child had been adopted from state care since 2019. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion The government has also been looking to establish an agency aimed at improving the protection of children from sexual abuse. The attorney general, Deb Frecklington, said a bill to establish the Queensland Protection Commission would be introduced to parliament on Wednesday, with the hope of having it launch in early 2027. The commission would be a “nation-leading” safeguarding agency for children and vulnerable people, bringing key child protection checks and safeguards under one roof, Frecklington said. “It is vitally important that we set up an agency … so we can push back on predators to make sure that Queensland children are kept very safe.” It came after a Child Death Review Board report found there were multiple opportunities missed to stop one of Australia’s most notorious paedophiles, Ashley Paul Griffith. https://www.politico.eu/article/factory-.text: SOUTHEASTERN UKRAINE — Two soldiers emerged from the tree line carrying the drone, trying to avoid scraping its wings against the branches. They placed it on the launch rail, angled toward the open sky above a field of budding sunflowers. The drone sprang to life, its small, rear-facing propeller roaring like a lawnmower. Sporadic raindrops pitter-pattered on the aircraft as the Ukrainian operators waited for their launch window. Then, at the press of a button, the drone shot into the gray sky for its final test flight before deployment to the front lines — where it would be sent to hunt. Advertisement Advertisement Drones have radically transformed the war in Ukraine. To capture how uncrewed aircraft are reshaping combat and how lessons from the fight are changing the way companies build these weapons, Business Insider — which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network — followed a Western-made AR3 surveillance drone from its factory in Wales to the battlefield in southeastern Ukraine, where soldiers from the 15th Artillery Reconnaissance "Black Forest" Brigade readied it for front-line operations. Its journey from production to the front underscores one of the central dynamics defining both the conflict and Western military and industrial planning. Ukraine still needs foreign aircraft to sustain its fight, while Western manufacturers need Ukrainian combat experience to keep those aircraft relevant against evolving Russian defenses. There's a deeper lesson in the manufacturing-and-feedback loop as NATO braces for its own potential fight. Sarmat, a platoon commander in the Black Forest Brigade who requested to be identified only by his call sign for security reasons, said that although Ukraine can produce millions of drones each year, its forces still need more aircraft and combat capability than the country can supply on its own. With Western-supplied drones, he said, "we have the opportunity to fly more, to detect more and to be much more successful." A factory on the Welsh coast At a private airfield on the Welsh coast, factory workers assemble AR3 drones inside one of several manufacturing sites in Britain that are operated by the Portuguese defense company Tekever. The long World War II-era runway and private airspace around the quaint town of Cardigan make it an ideal location for flight testing. Advertisement Advertisement Many of the drones produced here will soon embark on a nearly 2,000-mile journey east to Ukraine. One AR3 aircraft takes three to four weeks to produce, and roughly half of Tekever's drones go to Ukraine, said Rhys Hodges, the production lead at the facility. Before Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Tekever made reconnaissance drones for governments and commercial clients to monitor illegal fishing and migration at sea. Now, the company is increasingly producing uncrewed aircraft for Ukraine. Tekever is increasingly producing uncrewed aircraft for Ukraine. | Jake Epstein At the start of the war, Ukraine relied heavily on Western military assistance to fend off Russia's invasion forces. Kyiv also invested heavily in its own drone industry to gain a technological advantage over a much larger military. Hundreds of Ukrainian companies now produce millions of aircraft annually, including strike and reconnaissance drones. That growth has reduced Ukraine's dependence on foreign suppliers for some types of drones, but it has not eliminated it. Longer-range reconnaissance aircraft such as the AR3 can fly deeper and stay aloft longer than many of the smaller, cheaper drones that Ukraine produces in vast numbers. These tools give commanders a key way to locate valuable Russian targets beyond the immediate front. Ukrainian drone production and battlefield tactics are also shaping Western military planning and training. Top NATO officials have said they are absorbing many lessons from the conflict, including how quickly drone designs and countermeasures become obsolete. Advertisement Advertisement Western support is "extremely important to Ukraine," said Scott McClelland, the deputy director of Tekever's defense unit. "This ultimately comes down to wider European security." The U.K. is one of the largest suppliers of military aid and security assistance to Ukraine. It has committed more than $21 billion in military support since 2022, including 150,000 strike, reconnaissance and logistics drones this year. Tekever's AR3, the specific cost of which the company declined to provide, is among the systems supplied through that support, along with drones from British drone makers Windracers and Malloy Aeronautics. Sarmat's unit received its first AR3 in early 2024 and learned to operate the aircraft from Tekever. But the conversation doesn't end there. Tekever maintains a secure hotline around the clock to answer questions from Ukrainian operators. The soldiers, in turn, test new technology in combat and tell the company what needs to change to make the drone more effective. Exchanges like these, between troops and industry, have given rise to an accelerated development cycle driven by the brutal demands of modern warfare. A drone that works against Russian defenses today may struggle once Russia changes its jamming, detection or interception tactics. Manufacturers must then modify the aircraft before the advantage disappears. McClelland said that the feedback from Ukraine allows Tekever to continually upgrade the drone. For instance, after the Black Forest Brigade requested a change to the AR3's climb rate, the company modified the engine. Advertisement Advertisement "The operating environment in Ukraine has really required us to respond at a speed that is almost alien to traditional Western procurement," said McClelland. Western militaries might spend years bringing a new product to life and putting it into service with the armed forces. For Ukraine, that would be "far, far too late, " he said. Technology developed on that timeline could be "completely redundant" by the time it reached the battlefield because Russian forces and the conditions of the war would have already changed, creating new requirements. The pressure to move at speed and remain on the cutting edge extends beyond a single drone or type of drone. Western governments are studying how to shorten weapons development and procurement cycles for future conflicts in which equipment may need to be updated within months or weeks, rather than years. Ukraine is providing a real-time test of whether defense companies and procurement systems can keep pace. The pressure to move at speed and remain on the cutting edge extends beyond a single drone or type of drone. | Jake Epstein From Wales, the drones are boxed and sent to Portugal; then begins the long overland journey across Europe to Poland, where they cross into Ukraine. Tekever did not disclose specific shipping details for security reasons. To front-line units in Ukraine After a drive from the factory in Wales to London, a flight to Warsaw, two trains to Kyiv, and a final drive to a remote forest at the end of a dirt road near Dnipro — more than 24 hours of movement east — Business Insider caught up with one of Tekever's drones. The Black Forest Brigade uses the forest as cover when setting up AR3 drones for operations. Advertisement Advertisement The soldiers had also strung up camouflage netting to conceal their position from Russian drones that could be nearby. They carried assault rifles and electronic-warfare equipment as a last line of defense. The soldiers pulled a box from a windowless van that had been driven from Portugal with their drone. The vehicle also served as the aircraft's ground-control station. Slightly beyond the tree line, the Ukrainians assembled a catapult launch rail and communications antennae, then put together the AR3 like a Lego set, piece by piece, and ran a number of preflight checks under the cover of their camouflage netting. After securing the aircraft on the rail and waiting for a light rain shower to pass, the operators received clearance to launch. The drone, powered by its gas engine, took off into the sky. A few minutes later, it deployed a parachute and floated down onto the field before landing on an airbag. Two soldiers scrambled across to retrieve it. This was only a test flight — a final check before a real mission against Russian forces. On an operational flight, the AR3 can remain airborne for hours. It typically operates dozens of miles behind the front lines, searching for high-value targets such as air defense systems, radars and artillery, said Sarmat. Advertisement Operators pass the coordinates they collect to artillery crews, who can then decide whether to engage. The drone can return later to conduct a battle damage assessment should offensive units opt to open fire. That work fills a critical gap between the smaller drones watching the immediate front and other surveillance systems looking much farther into Russian-held territory. Operational tempo is high. The team works nonstop, sometimes more than seven days without a rest. Summer is ideal for reconnaissance; cameras are less effective in the winter, and the unit doesn't fly in bad weather. The battlefield has changed dramatically since the war began in 2022. | Jake Epstein "Every week, we have a lot of targets," said Sarmat. Shifting Russian tactics The battlefield has changed dramatically since the war began in 2022. It is now saturated with electronic warfare, which can disrupt flight operations for drones like the AR3 that rely on radio-frequency connections vulnerable to signal jamming. A drone does not need to be shot down to be rendered ineffective. If Russian forces sever its communications, interfere with its navigation or expose the operator's position, the mission may fail and leave the crew at risk. Advertisement Tekever declined to say how many of its AR3s have been lost in Ukraine. In August, Russian state media reported that Russian forces had downed an AR3 and transferred it to a research institute for study. Ukraine has been forced to explore innovative solutions to keep its drones in the sky. "It's war," said Sarmat. "Somebody has a shield — we create a sword. Then we create an automatic weapon. It's the same situation with electronic warfare." The work has become more dangerous for the Ukrainian operators. Every day, the drone-infested "kill zone" on the battlefield is expanding, putting even launch positions farther from the front within Russia's reach. That challenge can make concealment and mobility as important as the drones themselves at times. A sophisticated reconnaissance drone offers little advantage if Russian forces can find and attack the team launching it. Working from the forest is critical to the Black Forest Brigade's survival. Once, they lived in the trees for a month. Advertisement Mid-range reconnaissance drones like the AR3 help Ukraine find Russian forces and equipment behind the front lines. But as Ukraine leverages these Western-made weapons in the war, there's a deeper lesson in the cooperation for NATO. For alliance countries preparing for a possible large-scale confrontation with Russia, the lesson isn't simply that their militaries need drones. They may also need factories, purchasing systems and military institutions that can effectively act on front-line feedback, staying ahead of an adversary's swift adaptations. "Our main task is to win the war," said Sarmat. "But also, we have a task to give our partners all our experience and our advice on how to be successful on the front lines." https://www.dailystar.co.uk/news/latest-.text: Royal Mail has missed its delivery targets once again but said it was making progress to meet the goals as it rolls out a major overhaul to scrap second-class post on Saturdays. The group said it delivered 85% of first-class deliveries the next day and 91.4% of second-class mail within three working days during the first quarter of the year. Under targets set by Ofcom, 90% of first-class mail should be delivered the next day, and 95% of second-class mail should be delivered within three days. From April 1, the watchdog lowered previous delivery targets for first-class from 93% and second-class from 98.5% as part of universal service reforms. But Royal Mail insisted it had seen a marked improvement from a year earlier, when first quarter figures showed just 76% of first-class and 89.3% of second-class post arrived on time. The group - whose owner International Distribution Services was bought last year by Czech billionaire Daniel Kretinsky - recently pledged to meet the Ofcom delivery targets by May 2027 as part of a plan to invest £500 million in the service over the next five years. Last July, Ofcom gave postal reforms the green light to reflect steep declines in the number of letters being sent, allowing second-class letters to be delivered on alternate weekdays only. Royal Mail expects to complete the rollout of the new model across all its 1,200 delivery offices by Christmas , after initially being delayed until it had reached agreement with trade unions. Jamie Stephenson, Royal Mail chief operating officer, said: “These results are encouraging and show that the work we are doing to improve the service is having an impact. “First-class performance is well ahead of where we expected to be at this stage of our improvement plan, while second-class is tracking in line with the plan.” But he said “we know there is more to do”. Ofcom launched an investigation in June into Royal Mail’s failure to meet its delivery targets for the second year running in the 12 months to the end of March.
